amendment.text: New York City has its own toilet-count table (Table 403.1 of the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code), different from the state's. Occupants come from the NYC Building Code, are split half and half by sex, and fractions round up (403.1.1). Office counts are made per floor. Business (offices): a stepped schedule per sex: 1 to 20 persons 1 water closet, 21 to 45: 2, 46 to 70: 3, 71 to 100: 4, 101 to 140: 5, 141 to 190: 6, then 1 for each additional 50. Restaurants, banquet halls and food courts (A-2): 1 per 75 male, 1 per 75 female. Nightclubs, bars, taverns: 1 per 75 male, 1 per 40 female. Educational (E): 1 per 50 each sex. Urinals: not required; may replace up to 50% of required water closets in each toilet room (419.2). Separate facilities not required where the total of employees, customers, patrons and visitors is 30 or fewer (403.2). Public toilets not required for food service establishments with fewer than 20 seats and under 10,000 sq ft, nor for Group B or M establishments under 10,000 sq ft (403.3 exception). Each water closet used by the public or employees needs a compartment with a door (405.3.4); each urinal needs partitions from no more than 12 in to at least 60 in above the floor (405.3.5). No provision for multi-user all-gender toilet rooms.
amendment.quote: TABLE 403.1 MINIMUM NUMBER OF REQUIRED PLUMBING FIXTURES (See Sections 403.1.1 and 403.2) WATER CLOSETS (URINALS: SEE SECTION 419.2) MALE | FEMALE [...] A-2 Restaurants, banquet halls and food courts: 1 per 75 | 1 per 75 [...] Business B: No. of persons for each sex / No. of fixtures for each sex: 1-20: 1; 21-45: 2; 46-70: 3; 71-100: 4; 101-140: 5; 141-190: 6; 1 fixture for each additional 50 persons [...] Educational E: 1 per 50 | 1 per 50. | a. The occupant load for seasonal outdoor seating and entertainment areas shall be included when determining the minimum number of facilities required. | 403.1.1 Fixture calculations. To determine the occupant load of each sex, the total occupant load shall be divided in half. To determine the required number of fixtures, the fixture ratio or ratios for each fixture type shall be applied to the occupant load of each sex in accordance with Table 403.1. Fractional numbers resulting from applying the fixture ratios of Table 403.1 shall be rounded up to the next whole number. [...] Fixture calculations in Group B office occupancies shall utilize the total occupant load on a given floor to determine the number of fixtures required for that floor. | 403.2 Separate facilities. Where plumbing fixtures are required, separate facilities shall be provided for each sex. Exceptions: [...] 2. In structures or tenant spaces where combined employee and public toilet facilities are provided in accordance with Section 403.3, separate facilities shall not be required where the total number of employees, customers, patrons and visitors is 30 or fewer. | 403.3 [...] Exception: Public utilization of toilet facilities shall not be required for: 1. Food service establishments, as defined in Section 81.03 of the New York City Health Code, with a seating capacity of less than 20, provided such establishments are less than 10,000 square feet (929 m2). 2. Establishments less than 10,000 square feet (929 m2) classified as Occupancy Group B or M [...] | 405.3.4 Water closet compartment. The walls or partitions shall begin at a height not greater than 12 inches (305 mm) from and extend not less than 60 inches (1524 mm) above the finished floor surface. | 419.2 Substitution for water closets. In each bathroom or toilet room, urinals shall not be substituted for more than 50 percent of the required water closets.

restrooms_city.rule: Local Law 79 of 2016, now Administrative Code 28-315.9 and Plumbing Code 403.2.2 and 403.4: since January 1, 2017 every single-occupant toilet room in the city must be available to persons of any sex, existing rooms included, with a sign for all sexes near the entrance; no physical alteration is required beyond the sign. A single-occupant toilet room is an enclosed room with a securable door and no more than one water closet, one urinal and one lavatory. Exception: a room reached only through a room permissibly restricted by sex. The NYC Plumbing Code has no provision for multi-user all-gender toilet rooms: 403.2 requires separate facilities for each sex except for dwelling units and spaces serving 30 or fewer people, and 403.2.1 lets two family or assisted-use rooms serve as the separate facilities where each sex needs only one water closet.
restrooms_city.quote: 28-315.9 Single-occupant toilet rooms. Notwithstanding any other provision of law or rule requiring separate facilities for each sex, on and after January 1, 2017, all single-occupant toilet rooms shall be made available for use by persons of any sex in accordance with section 403.2.2 of the New York city plumbing code. Nothing in this section shall be construed to require physical alteration of a single-occupant toilet room except for the posting and maintenance of appropriate signage in accordance with section 403.4 such code. | PC 403.2.2 Single-occupant toilet rooms. All single-occupant toilet rooms shall be made available for use by persons of any sex. Existing toilet rooms shall comply with this section. [...] Exception: Where egress from a single-occupant toilet room is through a room permissibly restricted by sex. | PC 403.4 Signage. Required public facilities shall be designated by a legible sign for each sex or, for a single-occupant toilet room, for all sexes. Signs shall be readily visible and located near the entrance to each toilet facility. Existing single-occupant toilet rooms shall comply with this requirement. | PC 202 SINGLE-OCCUPANT TOILET ROOM. An enclosed space defined by walls and having a securable door that does not contain fixtures in excess of one water closet, one urinal, and one lavatory which is intended to be used by a single individual independently or an individual requiring assistance. The water closet shall not be within a secondary enclosure.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to New York City job sites. Price your restroom, see the city's own toilet counts and the rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for New York City office towers, schools, restaurants and theaters, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.access_bullet: - **Wheelchair access:** a restroom with stalls needs at least one stall a wheelchair user can enter and use. Federal law and New York City's building rules both set the sizes. A room with six or more toilets and urinals in total also needs a second accessible stall, 36 inches wide with grab bars on both sides. The city's access rules apply to alterations of older buildings too, minor ones included, but not to ordinary repairs.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** New York City has its own building rules. They treat toilet partitions as an interior wall finish and require solid plastic (HDPE) and polypropylene partitions to pass a room-corner fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** New York City has its own plumbing rules, separate from the state's. They set the number of toilets by how many people use the building, and every toilet used by staff or the public needs a stall with a door. The table further down shows what that means.
page.state_extra_bullet: - **New York City extras:** the city adds a vertical grab bar, 18 inches or longer, on the side wall beside each accessible toilet. The wheelchair turning space in the room can't be inside a stall.
extra_rule_bullets: - **New rules on July 17, 2027:** New York City's first building rules written for work in existing buildings take effect, and the 1968 rules that owners of older buildings may still choose today are repealed. For a project filed after that date, confirm which rules apply with the NYC Department of Buildings.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** in New York City every one-person restroom must be open to people of any sex, with a sign near the door that says so. That covers existing rooms, and the sign is the only change required. A one-person restroom is a lockable room with no more than one toilet, one urinal and one sink. Where a building needs more toilets than that, the city's plumbing rules call for separate men's and women's rooms unless the space serves 30 people or fewer. They have no rule for a shared all-gender room with several stalls, so ask the NYC Department of Buildings before you plan one.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** New York City requires a permit for most construction and alteration work. Minor alterations and ordinary repairs need none, but work that affects exits, fire safety or the building's accessibility requirements doesn't count as minor. The city's examples of work without a permit are painting, plastering, new cabinets, replacing a plumbing fixture and resurfacing floors. Toilet partitions aren't named in any of its lists, so ask the NYC Department of Buildings (212-566-5000) or your architect or engineer whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.stalls_intro: New York City counts toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. Half are counted as men and half as women, and any fraction rounds up. In an office building the count is made floor by floor. Every toilet needs its own stall with a door. Urinals are optional: in each men's room they can replace up to half of the required toilets. Each urinal needs a privacy screen that starts no more than 12 inches above the floor and reaches at least 5 feet.
page.stalls_after: These are minimums. The office figures are for one floor that holds that many people; the restaurant and school figures are for the whole building. A space for 30 people or fewer doesn't need separate men's and women's rooms. A restaurant's count includes seasonal outdoor seating, and a restaurant with fewer than 20 seats and under 10,000 square feet doesn't have to offer its toilets to the public. Neither does an office or store under 10,000 square feet, though staff toilets are still required. Bars and nightclubs need more women's toilets than restaurants: one for every 40 women. At least one stall in each room must be wheelchair accessible.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, New York City's building rules count an office at one person per 100 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room with tables and chairs at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20.

page.install_rule: New York City registers general contractors through the Department of Buildings and asks them for at least $1 million in general liability insurance. The department's pages tie that registration to contractors who build one- to three-family homes and don't say what interior work in a commercial building needs. New York State has no license for partition installers. Confirm what your job needs with the NYC Department of Buildings. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: New York State has no license for partition installers, so ask the NYC Department of Buildings what your contractor needs.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on public work, such as school, city and state projects, New York law requires at least the prevailing wage for the trade, with no minimum contract size. In New York City the City Comptroller sets the rates each July. For a carpenter on commercial building work that is $60.05 an hour plus $50.83 in benefits, through June 30, 2027.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 8.875% in New York City: 4% state, 4.5% city and 0.375% for the regional transit district.
page.buyers_extra: - **Theaters, museums and event venues:** stainless steel or phenolic where crowds are heavy and the finish is on show.

notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether a like-for-like replacement of toilet partitions in a commercial restroom counts as a minor alteration or ordinary repair, so needs no permit (NYC Department of Buildings, 212-566-5000, or a borough office).

Check the office row of the toilet-count table by eye in the Plumbing Code PDF: its two stepped columns interleave in the text layer. The page reads it as 1 to 20 people of each sex: 1 toilet, 21 to 45: 2, 46 to 70: 3, 71 to 100: 4, 101 to 140: 5, 141 to 190: 6, then one per 50.

The office figures in the table treat each occupant figure as one floor, because the city counts offices floor by floor; a 400-person office spread over several floors needs more toilets in total than the 400 row shows.

Contractor rule: the project's local-rules entry says general contractors must register before working on permitted projects, but the Department of Buildings pages and the code tie that registration to new one- to three-family homes. The page follows the department's pages. Ask the Licensing Unit what a contractor installing partitions in a commercial building needs (safety registration, insurance).
